title: Old-Time Wood Ash Garden Uses
subtitle: Don't Waste Your Stove Ashes
items: Cool ashes in a metal can
intro: Old USDA Farmers' Bulletins treated wood ashes as a free source of potash and lime for the garden. Used lightly and on the right soil, the ashes from a winter of wood heat can still feed next year's beds instead of going in the trash.
desc: Old-time uses for wood ash in the garden: use only plain hardwood ash, cool it in a metal can, test your soil pH first and spread it thinly, never around potatoes or blueberries. A thrifty homestead habit from old USDA bulletins. Full list on the blog.

title: How to Pressure Can Soup
subtitle: Vegetable or Meat Soup, Safely
intro: Home-canned soup is a lifesaver on a cold, busy night, but it has to be done the tested way. These steps follow the soup procedure in the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning: pressure canning only, no thickeners or pasta, and add noodles or rice when you heat a jar to serve.
desc: How to pressure can homemade vegetable or meat soup: no noodles, rice or flour, fill jars halfway with solids, top with broth leaving 1 inch headspace and process pints 60 minutes, quarts 75. Safe, tested USDA home canning steps. Full list on the blog.

title: First Backyard Flock Checklist
subtitle: Plan the Coop Before the Chicks
items: 4 sq ft per hen in the coop
8-10 sq ft per hen in the run
desc: Backyard chickens for beginners: a first flock checklist with coop and run space per hen, nest boxes, roost length and predator-proof hardware cloth, so you can plan this winter and be ready for spring chicks. (Contains affiliate links.)

title: Make a Seed Starting Calendar
subtitle: Count Back From Your Last Frost
items: Write every date on a calendar
intro: Winter is the time to plan when each crop gets started indoors. Count back from your average last frost date and you will know exactly which seeds to sow in January, February and March, with no rushing and no leggy seedlings.
desc: How to make a seed starting calendar: find your last frost date, then count back, onions 8-12 weeks, peppers 8-10, tomatoes 6-8 and cabbage family 4-6 weeks before. Easy winter vegetable garden planning for beginners. Full list on the blog.

title: How to Freeze Butter & Cheese
subtitle: Stock Up on Sale for Winter
items: Overwrap in foil or a bag
intro: Holiday sales are the best time to stock up on butter and cheese, and both freeze well if you wrap them right. Hard cheese turns a little crumbly after freezing, so save it for casseroles, soups and baking.
desc: How to freeze butter and cheese: keep butter in its wrapper and overwrap it, freeze hard cheese in 8 oz blocks or shredded, thaw in the fridge and cook with it. Stock up on holiday sales for your winter pantry. Full list on the blog.

title: Kitchen Scraps Hens Can Eat
subtitle: Safe Treats for Backyard Chickens
intro: Old farm flocks lived partly on kitchen scraps, and hens still love them. Keep treats small next to a complete layer feed, skip the few foods that can hurt them, and clear away leftovers so you don't feed rats too.
desc: Which kitchen scraps can chickens eat? Greens, squash and pumpkin are great, but skip avocado pits and skins, raw dry beans, moldy or salty food and chocolate, and keep treats under 10% of the diet. Backyard chicken tips for beginners. Full list on the blog.
